KEY MESSAGE 1...

Latest water vapor imagery shows our parent trough centered just north
of the Great Lakes with a secondary shortwave rounding the base
through the Ohio Valley. An area of rain and thunderstorms 
continues to push through PA early this morning ahead of the 
occluded boundary within a region of diffluent flow downstream 
of the trough. However, high res and deterministic guidance is 
in good agreement showing these showers/storms continuing to
weaken as they advance north and eastward through sunrise as 
they outrun the best forcing for ascent. While a few isolated 
showers develop ahead of the occluded front before sunrise, the
weakening area of showers/embedded storms should reach eastern 
NY and western New England 09 - 15 UTC this morning. The 
occluded boundary essentially stalls over eastern NY today with
the secondary shortwave from the Ohio Valley continuing to 
rotate into the Northeast, reaching eastern NY by early 
afternoon. As stronger height falls arrive, expecting scattered
clusters of showers/storms to redevelop and track from west to 
east. Forecast soundings and moisture profiles also show dry 
air surges into eastern NY/western New England this afternoon as
this stronger shortwave arrives. This will help steepen mid- 
level lapse rates over 6C/km with DCAPE values also rising over 
1000 J/kg. The incoming dry air should also help morning 
stratus break for sun with dew points in the mid to upper 60s 
supporting sfc-based instability increasing towards 1000 - 1500
J/kg per the REFS and CAMs. Given the incoming closed low, 
0-6km shear impressively reaches 40-50kts and 0-3km shear 
25-30kts.

Despite these favorable ingredients for severe weather, clouds 
look to break for sun just as the stronger height falls arrive, 
limiting the time for the atmosphere to destabilize before 
convective initiates. In addition, low-level forcing is limited 
to a weakening warm front lifting northward along a washout 
occluded front. These help explain why the HREF and REFS both 
only show low probabilities for updraft helicity values 
exceeding 20m/s mainly 20 - 00 UTC. This indicates that even as
isolated to scattered storm clusters initiate mid to late 
afternoon into the early evening hours, there should only be 
isolated instances of severe thunderstorms. Given weak updraft
growth, there are also questions if any storms can tap into the
stronger shear aloft. This matches with SPC's marginal risk 
(level 1 of 5) in their Day 1 Convective Outlook. Damaging winds
remain the primary hazard from any severe storms that form but 
any storm can also produce frequent lightning as forecast soundings
show sufficient instability extending into the favored -10C to -30C
region likely due to the cool/dry air tracking in aloft. Storms
can also produce heavy downpours given PWATs over 1". Convection
dissipates by 0 - 02 UTC with clouds clearing quickly thereafter,
supporting radiational fog overnight where heavy rain fell.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

Our mature closed low slowly propagates into southern Quebec by
Monday with its cool pool extending into eastern NY and western
New England. Southwest flow aloft will maintain elevated dew
points in the mid 50s to low 60s with the 500hPa -15C to -18C
cool pool aloft supporting steeper mid-level lapse rates 6 - 
6.5C/km with morning sun contributing to SB-CAPE values reaching
500 - 1000 J/kg. As a stronger shortwave rotates around the 
base of the closed low late Monday morning into the afternoon, 
stronger forcing for ascent should support a more organized area
of rain and even embedded thunderstorms tracking west to east. 
Given the cool pool, storms will not need to become too tall 
before lightning develops with any taller updrafts capable of 
small hail. However, forecast soundings shows low EL heights 
indicating low-topped convection and thus limiting severe 
weather potential. 

Winds shift westerly by Monday evening in the wake of the
shortwave with cool air advection over the still warm lakes 
supporting a lake effect and upslope rain response. Therefore, 
we continue to show likely and categorical POPs in the western 
Adirondacks with chance POPs in the southern Greens and Mohawk 
Valley. Westerly flow and the trough axis/cool pool under our 
very slow moving closed low should maintain at least scattered 
showers during the day on Tuesday favored near and north of 
I-90. The western Adirondacks and southern Greens will likely 
receive the highest rainfall amounts. Instability wanes by 
Tuesday so any storms should be isolated.

KEY MESSAGE 3...

High pressure builds back overhead by Wednesday supporting 
pleasant and dry conditions. However, the dry break does not 
last long as yet another shortwave trough approaches the 
Northeast Thursday into Friday. Southwest flow ahead of it will 
allow humidity levels to rise once again with temperatures 
trending slightly above normal. Heights fall in response to the
